newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Racism continues to stain Australia - commissioner.
newsitem.headline: Racism continues to stain Australia - commissioner.

text.p: Racism is staining Australia and is the cause of the nation's greatest failures, Human Rights Commissioner Chris Sidoti said on Sunday, citing the plight of Aborigines and a rise in complaints of racial discrimination.
"Our most significant failures as a nation...all seem to have a racial basis," said Sidoti, the national human rights commissioner, in a speech to mark U.N. Human Rights Day.
"Indigenous people are still the most disadvantaged by any measure...their treatment remains the wrongdoing on which today's Australia was built," Sidoti said.
"Racism is a continuing stain that has discredited our history and continues to infect our present," he said.
"The current racist episode has caused great damage to many of our fellow Australians and others who share the country with us, and indeed to our society itself," he said.

Australia has been engulfed in a debate on race since September when maverick politican Pauline Hanson made her maiden parliamentary speech, in which she charged that Australia was being swamped by Asians and that Aborigines had gained preferential treatment.
Asians make up 4.7 percent of the 18 million population and about one third of the annual 100,000 migrants.

Australia's white settlers, who first arrived in 1788, massacred, poisoned and hunted Aborigines. A government assimilation policy led to the forced separation of tens of thousands of aboriginal children from their parents until the policy ended in the 1960s. Aboriginal life expectancy is 10 to 15 years shorter than non-indigenous Australians.
Sidoti said that Australia's shortcomings in human rights also related to its treatment of children, unemployment, homelessness and the abuse of the elderly.
He said the number of complaints of race discrimination had reached record levels in recent months.
"Our Human Rights Commission has been told of racist abuse and violence often directed against children. Reports of racism in school playgrounds are especially worrying," Sidoti said.
Many recent racist remarks had been "justified as an exercise of free speech", he said.
"But what we've been experiencing hasn't been debate," Sidoti said. "Debate requires logic, facts and rational argument. We haven't heard debate, we've heard pure racism."
"It will take some time to heal the wounds our community has suffered this past year."
Australian Prime Minister John Howard has defended the race debate on the basis of freedom of speech but has been criticised across the political spectrum for allowing it to continue.
